                  RESPONSE TO APPLICANTS’ OBJECTIONS TO
                    DIRECT TESTIMONY OF STACY HODGE

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
        COMES NOW, Ryan and Stacy Hodge (Hodge) to timely file this Response to
Applicants’ Objections to Direct Testimony of Stacy Hodge (Interchange Item 4336)
and in support thereof respectfully show:

                                     I. Introduction

       Intervenors Ryan and Stacy Hodge file this response to Applicants’ objections
seeking to strike limited portions of Stacy Hodge’s direct testimony as hearsay and
improper non-expert opinion.
       Mrs. Hodge disclaimed offering expert medical or scientific causation testimony
and instead explained the basis for her family’s routing concerns and request for greater
separation from the proposed 765-kV line. That disclaimer is dispositive of Applicants’
Rule 702 objection and frames the proper lens for the hearsay analysis as well.
        The challenged statements are admissible because they are offered to show Mrs.
Hodge’s state of mind and the effect of information on her decision-making, not to prove
the truth of disputed scientific propositions.
       This testimony is offered only to explain Mrs. Hodge’s concern and routing
preference and not to establish that transmission lines cause leukemia or that any


                                             1
 particular exposure level is dangerous. Any disagreement with the underlying materials
she read goes to weight and can be addressed on cross-examination, not by exclusion.

                                            II. Background

       Mrs. Hodge is the mother of a young child with Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)
and testified about her family’s use of their home and yard and her resulting concern
about a proposed transmission line being routed close to their home.
        In the challenged passages, she stated that she read materials reporting (1) studies
describing an association between transmission line proximity and childhood leukemia,
(2) studies describing an association between magnetic-field exposure and childhood
leukemia, and (3) materials indicating children with Down syndrome have an elevated
baseline risk of leukemia and other blood cancers. She then explained that, based on what
she read and her daughter’s circumstances, she prefers feasible routing options that
provide greater separation.

                                            III. Argument

A. The Challenged Statements Are Not Hearsay Because They Are Offered to Show
   State of Mind and Effect on the Listener
        SOAH proceedings apply the Texas Rules of Evidence, but ALJs exercise broad
discretion in evaluating the weight and credibility of testimony in contested cases —
a standard that favors admission with appropriate weight-assignment over exclusion of
relevant lay testimony. 1
         Hearsay is an out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of the matter
asserted. 2 Hearsay is generally inadmissible unless an exception applies. 3 When a witness
testifies that she read or heard information and that it affected her concerns, motivations,
or decisions, the testimony is admissible to show its effect on the listener and the
witness’s state of mind—not for the truth of the underlying statement.
        The analysis follows a straightforward syllogism. Hearsay turns on whether a
statement is offered for its truth. Statements offered to show their effect on the listener
or the witness’s state of mind are not offered for their truth. The challenged passages
are introduced as “I read…” and “I began reading studies…” and are tied directly to



1
  See 1 Tex. Admin. Code § 155.429(a)(1) (SOAH rule providing that the Texas Rules of Evidence as
applied in a nonjury civil case in district court govern contested case hearings conducted by SOAH).
2
  Tex. R. Evid. 801(d).
3
  Id. R. 803.

     Ryan and Stacy Hodge; Response to Applicants’ Objections to Direct Testimony of Stacy Hodge
                                              2 of 7
 “therefore I am concerned and prefer more separation.” They are offered for effect on
the listener and state of mind, not truth.
         The probative point is not whether any study ultimately proves causation. The
relevant fact is that Mrs. Hodge encountered information that heightened her concern
as a parent of a medically vulnerable child and informed her routing preference.
Applicants may dispute the accuracy of what she read, but that dispute goes to weight,
not admissibility, because the operative fact is that she encountered the information and
it influenced her preference.
       Applicants remain free to cross-examine Mrs. Hodge about what she read, how
she understood it, and whether her concerns are well-founded.

B. The Challenged Statements Are Not Impermissible Expert Opinion Because
   Mrs. Hodge Does Not Offer Scientific Conclusions
        Mrs. Hodge expressly disclaimed offering expert medical or scientific testimony
or attempting to prove causation. She stated: “I am not offering expert testimony or
trying to prove causation. I am explaining the basis for my concern as a parent.” That
disclaimer clarifies the limited purpose of the testimony at the outset and is the most
direct answer to Applicants’ Tex. R. Evid. 702 objection.
         A lay witness may testify from personal knowledge and offer opinions rationally
based on her perceptions when helpful to understanding her testimony, so long as she
does not offer specialized scientific conclusions reserved for qualified experts. 4 To be
precise about what Mrs. Hodge is not doing: she does not calculate risk, interpret
statistical significance, compare competing studies, extrapolate from population data to
individual outcomes, or apply any specialized scientific methods to predict health effects
from this project. Her testimony is limited to her perceptions, what she encountered in
reading publicly available materials, and the resulting concern and routing preference.
That is the type of lay opinion Rule 701 permits when helpful to understand a witness’s
actions and decisions.
       Instead, she testifies to (1) what she read, (2) her daughter’s diagnosis and her
family’s circumstances, and (3) the resulting concern and routing preference. That is
permissible lay testimony about personal perception and decision-making, not expert
causation testimony.
        A concrete analogy illustrates the point: a parent who testifies about what a doctor
told her, what she read in discharge instructions, or what she understood about a child’s
diagnosis—offered to explain her later decisions and concerns rather than to prove the

4
    Id. R. 701, 702.

        Ryan and Stacy Hodge; Response to Applicants’ Objections to Direct Testimony of Stacy Hodge
                                                 3 of 7
 medical propositions themselves—is giving lay testimony grounded in personal
perception, not expert causation opinion. Mrs. Hodge’s testimony is of exactly that
character.

C. The Down Syndrome Baseline-Risk Testimony Is Grounded in Personal
   Knowledge and Is Distinct From Generic EMF–Leukemia Assertions
        Applicants’ objections treat all three challenged passages as equivalent “EMF
causes leukemia” claims. They are not.
         One of the challenged passages addresses a distinct point rooted in Mrs. Hodge’s
personal knowledge: her daughter Brynlee has been diagnosed with Down syndrome
(Trisomy 21), and through her experience as a registered nurse, as Brynlee’s parent,
and through discussions with medical providers and reading she has done in caring for her
daughter, Mrs. Hodge understands that children with Trisomy 21 may carry an elevated
baseline vulnerability to certain blood cancers compared to other children. That
understanding is grounded in her personal experience with her child’s condition and her
efforts to learn about it—not to introduce a medical treatise for its truth.
        Mrs. Hodge’s testimony on this point is carefully framed in state-of-mind terms.
She testified that she “had read that children with Down syndrome face elevated risk of
acute leukemias, including AML and ALL,” and that she “read in materials that children
with Down syndrome have an elevated baseline risk of leukemia and other blood cancers
than other children.” She does not measure that risk, attribute it to any particular
authority, or ask the ALJs to credit it as scientific fact. The materials she read are not
offered for their truth; they are offered to explain why her awareness of Brynlee’s
heightened vulnerability informs the degree of caution she exercises. The ALJs need not
resolve any scientific dispute to credit that parental concern.
        This baseline-risk context is analytically separable from any contested debate
about whether EMF exposure increases leukemia risk in the general population. Even if
the ALJs limited or disregarded generalized EMF–leukemia assertions, the Down
syndrome context can still be considered as part of the family-specific circumstances
that inform routing preference and the request for greater separation. That part of Mrs.
Hodge’s testimony stands on its own as admissible lay testimony about her child’s
diagnosis and her resulting parental concern.

D. The Testimony Is Relevant to Routing, Consistent With the Commission’s
   Prudent Avoidance Approach, and Supports Meaningful Public Participation
       Mrs. Hodge’s testimony is directly relevant to routing in this proceeding
independent of any scientific debate. A landowner’s family circumstances and the reasons

    Ryan and Stacy Hodge; Response to Applicants’ Objections to Direct Testimony of Stacy Hodge
                                             4 of 7
 she prefers greater separation make it more likely that the preference is genuine and
explain why distance matters to that specific household. That is relevant to assessing
routing impacts and the comparative evaluation of route alternatives. The Commission
routinely considers the nature and sensitivity of land uses affected by proposed routing—
and a home occupied by a medically vulnerable child is precisely the kind of circumstance
that informs that evaluation.
         The Commission has adopted a prudent avoidance policy for electric and
magnetic fields, recognizing that reasonable steps to reduce exposure may be appropriate
where feasible even without definitive proof of causation. 5 The Commission’s routing
criteria require consideration of the impact on the affected community and landowners,
and the governing statute directs the Commission to weigh factors including community
values and environmental integrity in the CCN determination. 6 A home occupied by a
child with a diagnosed medical vulnerability is squarely within the community values and
affected-landowner-impact considerations the Commission must address. Mrs. Hodge’s
testimony — explaining her family’s specific medical circumstances and the basis for her
separation preference — fits squarely within this framework.
       Mrs. Hodge is asking the Commission to consider feasible routing options that
provide greater separation from her home given her child’s established medical
vulnerability—not to find that the line will cause harm.
        Administrative routing proceedings exist precisely to allow affected residents to
present their circumstances and concerns to decision-makers. Excluding this testimony
would undermine that purpose without meaningfully advancing the reliability of the
record.

E. The Probative Value of Mrs. Hodge’s Testimony Substantially Outweighs Any
   Risk of Unfair Prejudice or Confusion
        Even if the ALJs evaluate admissibility under a prejudice-balancing framework
similar to Texas Rule of Evidence 403, Mrs. Hodge’s testimony easily clears that
threshold in this forum.
       The probative value is concrete and direct. Mrs. Hodge is an affected landowner
whose home and family circumstances bear on the routing evaluation the Commission is
conducting. Her testimony explains why greater separation from the proposed 765-kV
line matters specifically to her household — not in the abstract, but because of her
daughter’s diagnosed condition and her resulting parental concern. That explanation is


5
    See 16 Tex. Admin. Code §§ 25.101(a)(6), (b)(3)(B)(iv).
6
    Tex. Util. Code § 37.056(c)(4)(A), (D); 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.101(b)(3)(B).

        Ryan and Stacy Hodge; Response to Applicants’ Objections to Direct Testimony of Stacy Hodge
                                                 5 of 7
 directly relevant to assessing routing impacts on the affected area and the comparative
weight to assign her preference for greater separation. Without it, her routing preference
seems unexplained; with it, the Commission has the factual context necessary to evaluate
it properly.
        The risk of unfair prejudice is minimal and manageable. Mrs. Hodge has
disclaimed causation testimony and framed her statements as personal concern, not
scientific proof. The ALJs, in a contested case proceeding, are not a lay jury susceptible to
being inflamed by a parent’s concern about her child’s health. Administrative tribunals
are routinely expected to receive and weigh this testimony without treating a witness’s
expressed concern as proof of an underlying scientific proposition. 7 Any residual risk of
confusion is addressed by the limiting purpose already stated on the face of the testimony
itself.
        Striking the testimony entirely would impose a cost disproportionate to any
evidentiary concern: it would require ordinary landowners to retain and qualify expert
witnesses simply to explain why they are worried and why their family circumstances
make greater separation preferable. That result is inconsistent with the Commission’s
public participation framework and the purpose of contested case proceedings before
SOAH, which exist in part to give affected residents a meaningful opportunity to present
their circumstances to decision-makers.

                                            IV. Conclusion

        Applicants’ motion to strike should be denied in its entirety. Each challenged
passage is independently admissible: the statements about what Mrs. Hodge read are
offered to show her state of mind and the effect of that information on her routing
preference, not for the truth of any scientific proposition; the Down syndrome baseline-
risk passage is grounded in Mrs. Hodge’s personal knowledge of her own child’s diagnosis
and her parental experience, not in scientific causation; and her family circumstances and
stated reasons for preferring greater separation are directly relevant to the routing impacts
and comparative route evaluation the Commission must conduct. Mrs. Hodge disclaimed
expert and causation testimony, and her statements are admissible for their limited, stated
purpose. Excluding them would not advance the reliability of the record — it would
require an affected landowner to hire a scientific expert simply to explain why her family’s
circumstances make greater separation matter, and would undermine the public-
participation function this proceeding exists to serve.

7
  See Tex. Gov't Code § 2001.081 (establishing relaxed evidentiary standard in contested cases before state
agencies, permitting evidence of a type on which a reasonably prudent person commonly relies).
